column8: Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the Siege of Tyre, fought in 332 BCE on the coast of what is now Lebanon. On one side was Alexander the Great, king of Macedon, with his army and, later, a fleet of ships from the cities that had joined him. On the other was Tyre, a Phoenician city built on an island, with its walls, its harbours and its fleet. The siege lasted about seven months.

Siege of Tyre. In 332 BCE, Alexander of Macedon tried to take the island city of Tyre. To reach it, his men built a road of stone and earth across the sea. The Tyrians fought back by sea, by fire and with machines of their own. After about seven months, the city fell. That road across the sea is called a mole: a bank of stones and earth built out into the water. Sand later piled up against it. The island of Tyre is joined to the mainland to this day.

After Issus. In late 333 BCE, Alexander defeated the Persian king, Darius the Third, at Issus, in the corner between Asia Minor and Syria. Then he marched south, down the coast of Phoenicia, the land of the great trading cities of the Levant. One by one, the Phoenician cities came over to him. AR-a-dus did, and Byblos. The people of Sidon invited him in. Tyre also sent envoys to meet him on the road. Among them was the son of the king. They said that Tyre would do whatever Alexander commanded. The king himself, Azz-em-ILL-kus, was not at home. He was at sea, with his ships, in the Persian fleet. Alexander had a reason to want every port on this coast. The Persian fleet was mostly Phoenician and Cypriot ships. If the ports were his, Arry-an has him say, that fleet would have nowhere to go, and the road to Egypt would be open.

The island city. Tyre stood on a rocky island, a little way off the coast. Dye-o-DOR-us says four stades of sea lay between them: about seven hundred metres. A modern study reconstructs the island as about one and a half kilometres long and six hundred metres wide. High walls ran all round it. On the side facing the mainland, Arry-an says they were about a hundred and fifty feet high, built of large stones set in mortar. The city had two harbours: one facing north, toward Sidon, and one facing south, toward Egypt. Its oldest and holiest place was the temple of its god Mel-kart, whom the Greeks called Heracles. Arry-an calls it the most ancient temple in human memory. On the mainland opposite stood an older settlement, called Old Tyre. Tyre was a city of seafarers. Its colonists had founded Carthage, in North Africa, and the two cities still kept close ties.

The refusal. Alexander said he wished to enter Tyre and sacrifice to Heracles in his temple. The Tyrians gave their answer. Arry-an reports it like this: they would do anything else he asked, but they would let neither Persians nor Macedonians into their city, while the war was still undecided. KUR-shus adds an offer. There was a temple of Hercules on the mainland, at Old Tyre, the envoys said. Alexander could sacrifice there. The writers explain the refusal differently. In Arry-an, it reads as a city trying to stay out of a war between two great powers. Dye-o-DOR-us says the Tyrians wanted to please Darius, trusted in their island, and hoped for help from Carthage. Alexander sent the envoys away. KUR-shus alone says that, later, heralds sent to urge peace were killed and thrown into the sea. No other surviving writer tells this.

The two sides. How many men Alexander had at Tyre, no ancient writer reliably says. Nor do they count the city's defenders. This page gives no army numbers. What Alexander had was the army that had won at Issus. What he did not have was a fleet that could face Tyre's. Tyre had walls, engines, and, Dye-o-DOR-us says, eighty try-reems: warships rowed by three banks of oars, with a bronze ram at the bow. It also had smaller boats that could carry archers, slingers and catapults. The Tyrians voted to send their children, their women and their old people to Carthage. Dye-o-DOR-us says only a part of them got away before the siege closed in. KUR-shus tells the same story. The rest stayed in the city. Dye-o-DOR-us says the Tyrians mocked Alexander. Did he think he could overcome Poseidon, the god of the sea?

Our four main writers lived hundreds of years later: Dye-o-DOR-us of Sicily, in the first century BCE; KUR-shus and Plutarch, in the first and early second centuries CE; and Arry-an, in the second century CE. They used older histories that are now lost. They often disagree: about what happened, in what order, and how many died. When they do, this page tells you who says what. "Estimate" marks a rounded number, and "reconstruction" marks our own best placing on the map. The map follows Arry-an's order of events. Alexander decides to reach the island on foot. Arry-an says he dreamed that Heracles took him by the hand and led him into the city, and his seer, Arris-TAN-der, said that Tyre would fall, but only after great labour. His men start to build the mole out from the mainland, toward the city. Dye-o-DOR-us says they pulled down Old Tyre for its stones, and that people from the nearby towns were brought in to carry them. Arry-an describes the water: shallow and muddy near the shore, and about three fathoms deep, a little over five metres, close to the city. Stakes drive easily into the mud, and the mud binds the stones together. Dye-o-DOR-us gives the width of the mole as two plethra, about sixty metres. Near the shore, the work goes quickly.

The further the mole reaches, the deeper the water and the closer the walls. Now the builders are within range. Arry-an says the Tyrians still ruled the sea. From their try-reems they row up along the sides of the mole and strike at the workers. From the walls, they shoot down on them. The builders are not dressed for battle. Alexander answers with screens to shield them, and builds two towers at the head of the mole, covered with hides and skins, with engines on top to shoot back.

The Tyrians make a weapon of their own. They take an old horse transport, a wide ship, and fill it with dry wood, pitch and sulphur. On two masts they hang cauldrons of things that burn. They weigh down the stern, so that the bow rides high. Then they wait for a wind blowing toward the mole. Their try-reems tow the ship in, and set it alight. The crew swim away. The ship drives against the head of the mole, and both towers catch fire. Tyrian boats close in, tear up the stakes along the mole and burn the engines that the fire had missed. This is Arry-an's story. Alexander orders the mole made wider, so that it can carry more towers, and the work begins again.

Dye-o-DOR-us has no fireship. He tells instead of a great wind from the north-west, which smashed much of the mole. Alexander had whole trees cut in the mountains and brought down, branches and all, to rebuild it. Dye-o-DOR-us also tells of fear inside the city. Some Tyrians said that their god Apollo meant to leave them for Alexander, so they bound his statue with golden chains. Plutarch tells this story too. Whether the storm and the fireship were two blows or two tellings of one, no one can say.

Alexander goes to Sidon to gather ships. The kings of AR-a-dus and Byblos hear that their cities are now in his hands. They leave the Persian fleet, and bring their ships to him: about eighty Phoenician ships, with the ships of Sidon. Ten come from Rhodes, three each from Soli and MAL-us, in Asia Minor, and ten from Lycia. There is one Macedonian ship: a penteconter, a ship of fifty oars, under PRO-tee-as. Not long after, the kings of Cyprus sail in with about a hundred and twenty more. Arry-an's numbers add up to about two hundred and twenty-five ships. Plutarch rounds it to two hundred. Now Alexander, too, has a fleet. Many of its crews are Phoenician, like the Tyrians themselves.

While the ships are made ready, Alexander leaves Sidon. He takes some squadrons of cavalry, the archers, the Agrianians, light troops from the Balkans, and the hy-PASS-pists, the foot guards who fought close to the king. He marches into the Antilebanon mountains, against the Arab peoples there. Some places he takes by force; others come to terms. Within ten days he is back in Sidon, where four thousand Greek mercenaries have arrived to join him. Plutarch, quoting an older writer named Chares, tells a story from this march. Alexander's old tutor, Lye-SIM-a-kus, could not keep up, and Alexander risked his life to stay behind with him. It is a story about the king, told by his admirers.

Alexander sails for Tyre with his fleet in battle order. The Tyrians had meant to fight at sea. When they see how many ships are coming, they stay in harbour. They block both harbour mouths with their try-reems. At the north harbour, the Phoenicians ram three of them, and the crews swim ashore. Then Alexander sets his watch. The Cypriots, under the admiral An-DROM-a-kus, guard the harbour toward Sidon. The Phoenicians guard the harbour toward Egypt, on the far side of the mole, close to Alexander's own tent. The city is now shut in, by land and by sea.

Alexander now brings his engines by sea. He mounts them on horse transports and slow try-reems and moves them up to the walls. But many stones lie in the water at the foot of the walls, and they keep the ships away. Who put them there, Arry-an does not say. The Macedonians anchor and try to haul them out. Tyrian ships, covered with armour, row in and cut the anchor ropes. Alexander shields his anchors with armoured boats of his own. Then Tyrian divers swim out under the water and cut the ropes again. At last the Macedonians use chains instead of ropes. From the mole, they lasso the stones, drag them clear, and drop them into deep water.

On the walls, the Tyrians answer engine with engine. Dye-o-DOR-us describes their devices. Spinning wheels, divided into sections, to break the flight of bolts. Soft padding, and hides stuffed with seaweed, to soak up stones. Nets to snag the attackers, and hooked tridents on lines to drag them off the bridges. Long poles with blades to cut the ropes of the rams. And sand, heated red-hot in bronze shields and thrown down on the men below. It ran in under their armour. KUR-shus describes the hot sand too. Dye-o-DOR-us adds that the Tyrians built a second wall behind the first.

The Tyrians plan a surprise. Behind sails stretched across the mouth of the north harbour, they man thirteen of their best ships. Three are kwin-kwi-reems and three are kwod-ri-reems, warships larger than try-reems, with more rowers to each oar. Seven are try-reems. At midday, when many of the sailors outside are resting and Alexander has gone to his tent, they row out in silence, in single file. They fall on the Cypriot ships at anchor. At the first charge they sink the kwin-kwi-reem of King Nye-TAG-o-ras of Salamis, in Cyprus. Then they sink the ships of AN-dro-kleez of AM-a-thus and Pa-SICK-ra-teez of KYOO-ree-um, and drive others onto the shore. But Alexander comes back sooner than usual. He rows round the island with his own ships. The Tyrians on the walls shout and signal to their ships to come back. Few of them make it in time. Most of the Tyrian ships are disabled, and two are captured at the harbour mouth. Most of their crews swim to safety.

Now the rams go to work. On the side facing the mole, the wall is too strong, and they do nothing. On the side toward Sidon, nothing either. On the side facing south, toward Egypt, they shake the wall until part of it falls. Alexander sends men across on bridges from the ships. The Tyrians drive them back without much trouble. Dye-o-DOR-us tells it differently. In his account, a stretch of wall about thirty metres long falls, and the attackers burst in, but are thrown out, and the Tyrians rebuild the gap that same night. After this, he says, the mole reached the wall, and the city was joined to the land.

Alexander waits for calm weather. Then he brings the engine ships back to the south wall, and the rams open a wide breach. Two ships carry bridges. On one, commanded by Ad-MEE-tus, are the hy-PASS-pists. On the other, the infantry battalion of SEE-nus. The Tyrians fall back from the walls. Many gather to make a stand at a shrine of a-JEE-nor, a hero of Tyre. Dye-o-DOR-us says the Tyrians blocked their narrow streets and fought until almost all of them were cut down. KUR-shus says that some Sidonians, who had come with Alexander, hid Tyrians on board their ships and took them away to Sidon.

Some Tyrians reach the temple of Heracles, Mel-kart's temple. Among them are King Azz-em-ILL-kus, now back in his city, and the leading men of Tyre. With them are envoys from Carthage, who had come to honour Heracles, by an ancient custom, in their mother city. How or when the king came home from the Persian fleet, no source says. Alexander spares all who took refuge in the temple. Arry-an dates the fall of Tyre to the Athenian month of Heck-a-tom-BEE-on: about July or August of 332 BCE.

Tyre fell after about seven months. Dye-o-DOR-us, Plutarch and KUR-shus give that length. Arry-an dates the fall, but does not say how long the siege took. Each writer gives his own numbers for the Tyrians, and they cannot be added together. Arry-an says about eight thousand Tyrians were killed, and about thirty thousand were sold as slaves, Tyrians and foreigners caught in the city. Dye-o-DOR-us says more than seven thousand were killed in the street fighting. Afterwards, he says, Alexander had at least two thousand young men hung up and killed, and more than thirteen thousand were taken as slaves. KUR-shus says six thousand fighting men were killed in the city, and two thousand were crucified. He adds that fifteen thousand were saved, hidden by the Sidonians. On Alexander's side, Arry-an counts Ad-MEE-tus and twenty hy-PASS-pists killed in the final assault, and about four hundred Macedonians killed in the whole siege. Then Alexander made his sacrifice to Heracles in the temple he had asked to enter at the start. His army marched past in armour, and his fleet sailed past in review. There were games and a torch race in the temple grounds. In the temple he dedicated the engine that had broken the wall, and the sacred ship of Heracles that his fleet had captured. During the siege, Arry-an says, envoys from Darius had come with an offer of peace. Alexander turned it down. Alexander marched south. Gaza resisted him too. After Gaza, he entered Egypt. Some of the people Tyre sent away before the siege reached Carthage. Dye-o-DOR-us says that most of the women and children had gone there. KUR-shus says the Carthaginians had sent word that they could give no help. How many reached safety, no one can say. Tyre did not disappear. It was resettled and rebuilt, and became a busy port again under later Greek kings and under Rome. Most of the ruins on the old island today are Roman and Byzantine. The mole changed the coast for good. Sand carried along the shore piled up against it, and over the centuries the island became a peninsula. Dye-o-DOR-us says the city "became a peninsula" during the siege itself. The geologists say it took much longer, and that a sandy bank under the water had helped the builders from the start. Today Tyre, called Soor in Arabic, is a city in southern Lebanon. Its ancient ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The town stands on the sand that grew against Alexander's mole.

They weigh down the stern, so that the bow rides high. Then they wait for a wind blowing toward the mole. Their try-reems tow the ship in, and set it alight. The crew swim away. The ship drives against the head of the mole, and both towers catch fire. Tyrian boats close in, tear up the stakes along the mole and burn the engines that the fire had missed. This is Arry-an's story. Alexander orders the mole made wider, so that it can carry more towers, and the work begins again.

Dye-o-DOR-us has no fireship. He tells instead of a great wind from the north-west, which smashed much of the mole. Alexander had whole trees cut in the mountains and brought down, branches and all, to rebuild it. Dye-o-DOR-us also tells of fear inside the city. Some Tyrians said that their god Apollo meant to leave them for Alexander, so they bound his statue with golden chains. Plutarch tells this story too. Whether the storm and the fireship were two blows or two tellings of one, no one can say.

Alexander goes to Sidon to gather ships. The kings of AR-a-dus and Byblos hear that their cities are now in his hands. They leave the Persian fleet, and bring their ships to him: about eighty Phoenician ships, with the ships of Sidon. Ten come from Rhodes, three each from Soli and MAL-us, in Asia Minor, and ten from Lycia. There is one Macedonian ship: a penteconter, a ship of fifty oars, under PRO-tee-as. Not long after, the kings of Cyprus sail in with about a hundred and twenty more. Arry-an's numbers add up to about two hundred and twenty-five ships. Plutarch rounds it to two hundred. Now Alexander, too, has a fleet. Many of its crews are Phoenician, like the Tyrians themselves.

While the ships are made ready, Alexander leaves Sidon. He takes some squadrons of cavalry, the archers, the Agrianians, light troops from the Balkans, and the hy-PASS-pists, the foot guards who fought close to the king. He marches into the Antilebanon mountains, against the Arab peoples there. Some places he takes by force; others come to terms. Within ten days he is back in Sidon, where four thousand Greek mercenaries have arrived to join him. Plutarch, quoting an older writer named Chares, tells a story from this march. Alexander's old tutor, Lye-SIM-a-kus, could not keep up, and Alexander risked his life to stay behind with him. It is a story about the king, told by his admirers.

Alexander sails for Tyre with his fleet in battle order. The Tyrians had meant to fight at sea. When they see how many ships are coming, they stay in harbour. They block both harbour mouths with their try-reems. At the north harbour, the Phoenicians ram three of them, and the crews swim ashore. Then Alexander sets his watch. The Cypriots, under the admiral An-DROM-a-kus, guard the harbour toward Sidon. The Phoenicians guard the harbour toward Egypt, on the far side of the mole, close to Alexander's own tent. The city is now shut in, by land and by sea.

Alexander now brings his engines by sea. He mounts them on horse transports and slow try-reems and moves them up to the walls. But many stones lie in the water at the foot of the walls, and they keep the ships away. Who put them there, Arry-an does not say. The Macedonians anchor and try to haul them out. Tyrian ships, covered with armour, row in and cut the anchor ropes. Alexander shields his anchors with armoured boats of his own. Then Tyrian divers swim out under the water and cut the ropes again. At last the Macedonians use chains instead of ropes. From the mole, they lasso the stones, drag them clear, and drop them into deep water.

On the walls, the Tyrians answer engine with engine. Dye-o-DOR-us describes their devices. Spinning wheels, divided into sections, to break the flight of bolts. Soft padding, and hides stuffed with seaweed, to soak up stones. Nets to snag the attackers, and hooked tridents on lines to drag them off the bridges. Long poles with blades to cut the ropes of the rams. And sand, heated red-hot in bronze shields and thrown down on the men below. It ran in under their armour. KUR-shus describes the hot sand too. Dye-o-DOR-us adds that the Tyrians built a second wall behind the first.

The Tyrians plan a surprise. Behind sails stretched across the mouth of the north harbour, they man thirteen of their best ships. Three are kwin-kwi-reems and three are kwod-ri-reems, warships larger than try-reems, with more rowers to each oar. Seven are try-reems. At midday, when many of the sailors outside are resting and Alexander has gone to his tent, they row out in silence, in single file. They fall on the Cypriot ships at anchor. At the first charge they sink the kwin-kwi-reem of King Nye-TAG-o-ras of Salamis, in Cyprus. Then they sink the ships of AN-dro-kleez of AM-a-thus and Pa-SICK-ra-teez of KYOO-ree-um, and drive others onto the shore. But Alexander comes back sooner than usual. He rows round the island with his own ships. The Tyrians on the walls shout and signal to their ships to come back. Few of them make it in time. Most of the Tyrian ships are disabled, and two are captured at the harbour mouth. Most of their crews swim to safety.

Now the rams go to work. On the side facing the mole, the wall is too strong, and they do nothing. On the side toward Sidon, nothing either. On the side facing south, toward Egypt, they shake the wall until part of it falls. Alexander sends men across on bridges from the ships. The Tyrians drive them back without much trouble. Dye-o-DOR-us tells it differently. In his account, a stretch of wall about thirty metres long falls, and the attackers burst in, but are thrown out, and the Tyrians rebuild the gap that same night. After this, he says, the mole reached the wall, and the city was joined to the land.

Alexander waits for calm weather. Then he brings the engine ships back to the south wall, and the rams open a wide breach. Two ships carry bridges. On one, commanded by Ad-MEE-tus, are the hy-PASS-pists. On the other, the infantry battalion of SEE-nus. At the same time Alexander sends try-reems against both harbours, and ships with archers and catapults circle the walls. The bridges go down onto the rubble. Ad-MEE-tus is the first man onto the wall. A spear strikes him, and he falls dead. Alexander follows him up with his own men, and they take the wall. Dye-o-DOR-us tells this part differently too. In his account, Ad-MEE-tus died earlier, from the blow of an axe, in an attack that failed. That night, he says, Alexander thought of giving up the siege. In his account the city was finally entered near its shipyards. Plutarch adds a story about the day itself. Arris-TAN-der had promised that Tyre would fall within the month. On the last day of the month, with the city still standing, Alexander ordered that day counted as only the twenty-eighth, and pressed the attack.

At the south harbour, the one facing Egypt, the Phoenician squadron breaks through the booms, the floating barriers across its mouth. Inside, they ram the Tyrian ships afloat and drive others ashore. At the north harbour, which Arry-an says had no boom at all, the Cypriots sail straight in, and enter the city from that side. Tyre is now open from the south wall and from both its harbours.

The Tyrians fall back from the walls. Many gather to make a stand at a shrine of a-JEE-nor, a hero of Tyre. Arry-an says the Macedonians were enraged, by the long siege, and because the Tyrians had killed Macedonian prisoners on the walls, in sight of the camp, and thrown them into the sea. Dye-o-DOR-us says the Tyrians blocked their narrow streets and fought until almost all of them were cut down. KUR-shus says that some Sidonians, who had come with Alexander, hid Tyrians on board their ships and took them away to Sidon.

Some Tyrians reach the temple of Heracles, Mel-kart's temple. Among them are King Azz-em-ILL-kus, now back in his city, and the leading men of Tyre. With them are envoys from Carthage, who had come to honour Heracles, by an ancient custom, in their mother city. How or when the king came home from the Persian fleet, no source says. Alexander spares all who took refuge in the temple. Arry-an dates the fall of Tyre to the Athenian month of Heck-a-tom-BEE-on: about July or August of 332 BCE.

Tyre fell after about seven months. Dye-o-DOR-us, Plutarch and KUR-shus give that length. Arry-an dates the fall, but does not say how long the siege took. Each writer gives his own numbers for the Tyrians, and they cannot be added together. Arry-an says about eight thousand Tyrians were killed, and about thirty thousand were sold as slaves, Tyrians and foreigners caught in the city. Dye-o-DOR-us says more than seven thousand were killed in the street fighting. Afterwards, he says, Alexander had at least two thousand young men hung up and killed, and more than thirteen thousand were taken as slaves. KUR-shus says six thousand fighting men were killed in the city, and two thousand were crucified. He adds that fifteen thousand were saved, hidden by the Sidonians. On Alexander's side, Arry-an counts Ad-MEE-tus and twenty hy-PASS-pists killed in the final assault, and about four hundred Macedonians killed in the whole siege. Then Alexander made his sacrifice to Heracles in the temple he had asked to enter at the start. His army marched past in armour, and his fleet sailed past in review. There were games and a torch race in the temple grounds. In the temple he dedicated the engine that had broken the wall, and the sacred ship of Heracles that his fleet had captured. During the siege, Arry-an says, envoys from Darius had come with an offer of peace. Alexander turned it down. Alexander marched south. Gaza resisted him too. After Gaza, he entered Egypt. Some of the people Tyre sent away before the siege reached Carthage. Dye-o-DOR-us says that most of the women and children had gone there. KUR-shus says the Carthaginians had sent word that they could give no help. How many reached safety, no one can say. Tyre did not disappear. It was resettled and rebuilt, and became a busy port again under later Greek kings and under Rome. Most of the ruins on the old island today are Roman and Byzantine. The mole changed the coast for good. Sand carried along the shore piled up against it, and over the centuries the island became a peninsula. Dye-o-DOR-us says the city "became a peninsula" during the siege itself. The geologists say it took much longer, and that a sandy bank under the water had helped the builders from the start. Today Tyre, called Soor in Arabic, is a city in southern Lebanon. Its ancient ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The town stands on the sand that grew against Alexander's mole.
